doc.title: Terry Gibbs interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]

title: The Seville club and the first Dream Band nights
summary: He turned a five-piece booking at the failing Seville into a rehearsed fifteen-piece band; 300 people and movie stars came.

story.theme_name: Going west: California and the Los Angeles scene
story.community_name: Going west: moving to and working in California

blocks.x: Yeah. Well I was going to do this in the studio. This was done in the studio. But they want you in the studio, not rehearsing in a hall somewhere. So I had all this music. In the meantime there was a club that was going to close call The Seville. And the movie columnist called Eve Star took a liking to how I played and she knew the club owner at The Seville, and they were going to go out of business. They tried Latin, they tried all this, they had to try jazz. So they hired me with a quintet. They said five musicians. Now being an out-of-towner I got decent money. The scale was only $15 but I got much more than that, and we did — on a Tuesday night — we did fairly good for them. And so we did it again the next Tuesday. In the meantime I heard that you are allowed to rehearse for a nightclub engagement, even though you can’t for a record date, so what I did is I said to the guy, “How’d you like to have a fifteen piece band for what you’re paying me for five musicians?” Because I had enough. The scale was $15 at that time. I had enough to pay everybody scale. He says, “I don’t care if you get four million” he says, “we don’t do any business I’m going to close anyhow.” So I got a chance to rehearse. We expected 20 people, 25 people to come in the club. They sold 300 you know. The 20 people would have paid enough to maybe, with drinking and all, to pay the tab, which would have been the quintet. Steve Allen at that time was just a friend of mine. I didn’t work for him. He gave me a little plug. We recorded all day—I rehearsed it all, for two or three days. Went in the club. Sure enough like I thought, after all day, 20 people, that’s all we expected. I went in the back room, because all we had was 12 arrangements that we recorded, and in those days did three and four shows a night. So we went in the back room with the 12 © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

pieces of music and I said, “On this song on letter B, Conte you play a hundred choruses, on C Frank Rosolino, you have two thousand choruses,” we had to open it up. We’ll make backgrounds you know. And so we started to walk out to play, and there were 300 people packed in the club with a line waiting to get in. And you saw faces like Fred McMurray and Ginger Rodgers. All these movie stars. And all the musicians in town. So I called the band back in the dressing room. I said, “We’re starting a band tonight, but there’s one rule. There’s no drinking off the bandstand. If you want to drink you have to drink on stage.” You never saw a wilder scene in your life. The audience couldn’t get a drink. I turned around and saw Med Flory, “Here, I have to have a beer, Terry. Wait a second. Waitress.” We’d have five waitresses on the stage giving everybody beers, whatever they drink. The audience is waiting for a drink. But you couldn’t get in the club. And immediately we were the talk of Hollywood. So we said let’s do it again next week. Sure enough we come to work, 9:30, 20 people. We figured it was a fluke. Went in the back room, by that time Bill Holman lent me an arrangement, Med Flory lent me an arrangement, I had about sixteen arrangements. We had to talk over what we were going to do with that. And by the time we came out to play at 10:00, you couldn’t get in. Packed, a line around the corner. It was ridiculous. More movie stars. You know Louella Parsons, you know that name?
